summary.text:
The number that matters is Table 19. Financing costs are 14.52% of the net revenue stream in 2025/26 and forecast to reach 23.21% by 2027/28 — close to a quarter of everything from council tax, business rates and general grant. The CFR goes from £317.790m to £364.970m over the same period, driven by a capitalisation directive of £39.162m in 2025/26 and £48.754m forecast for 2026/27.

The balance sheet reconciles on four paths and their Table 14 gives five PWLB certainty rates for 31 March 2026 that match our series to the basis point — the third council to do that.

Unusually, their book is not in discount. Twenty of the twenty-eight loans price above par and the whole thing nets to about £1.2m of premium, because the coupons are mostly 4% and above rather than the sub-2% money most councils were writing before 2022. That makes it the nearest-to-par book we have read, and it means the rescheduling question is close to neutral for them in either direction.

Live item: £8m of LOBOs with rate-increase options every July and January, which they intend to repay if exercised.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the 2025/26 treasury outturn that went to Audit and Governance on 22 June. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

Two cross-checks first, both of which came out clean. Your Table 1 reconciles on every line — CFR £317.790m less borrowing of £245.679m gives the £72.111m you show, and taking off £62.246m of balance sheet resources gives the £9.865m of net borrowing. The CFR movement rebuilds too: £285.400m opening, plus £23.500m of capital expenditure and £39.160m of EFS, less £20.670m of grant and other funding and £9.600m of MRP, is £317.790m to the pound.

The second is more unusual. Your Table 14 gives six PWLB certainty rates for 31 March 2026, and five of them — 5.04, 5.28, 5.72, 6.23 and 6.08 — match our own series for that day to the basis point. You are the third council this summer to do that, and the other two are also Arlingclose clients. It is a small thing but it means when we say something about the market we are speaking the same language as your adviser.

What we actually wrote about is Table 19. Financing costs are 14.52% of the net revenue stream in 2025/26 and forecast at 18.80% next year and 23.21% in 2027/28 — approaching a quarter of everything that arrives from council tax, business rates and general grant. Your own paragraph 8.8 names the driver: "Fair Funding Review 2.0 has made the council more dependent on borrowing and without a significant change in funding the council will see the underlying need to borrow increase." The CFR follows, from £317.790m to £364.970m, with capitalisation directives of £39.162m and a forecast £48.754m behind it. We have no view on any of that; it is your position and you have set it out more plainly than most.

Where we might be useful is the bit that moves between reports. £42.000m of local authority borrowing sits at a weighted average maturity of 0.77 years and £33.000m of short-term money at 0.01 years, so £75m reprices more or less continuously. One-year certainty closed at 4.95% this afternoon on notice 314/26 against your 4.21% and 4.76% on those two lines, and July's sector borrowing was thin — £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%. When a fifth of the book turns over inside a year and financing costs are already 14.52% of net revenue, the level it turns over at is not a detail. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

One genuinely distinctive thing, offered because it runs against the grain. Almost every loan book we have priced this summer is deep in discount, because most of it was written before 2022 at coupons under 2%. Yours is not. Running your 28 PWLB loans through the DMO's premature repayment formula this afternoon, twenty of them price above par and the whole book nets to about £1.2m of premium on a £163.2m balance. That is the closest-to-par book we have come across, and it is simply a consequence of your coupons being mostly 4% and above. It means the rescheduling question is close to neutral for you in either direction, which is a useful thing to be able to say to members when it comes up. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis — indicative only, the DMO's quote is the one that binds, and we model no MRP or accounting treatment.

The live item is the £8m of LOBOs. Options to raise the rate every July and January, and paragraph 4.6 records that you would repay rather than accept revised terms. We have picked up five LOBO calls across the sector in a few months — Kent, Tameside, Newcastle, York and Barnet — and the pattern is lenders testing options now that PWLB rates have risen to meet them. Each January and July is a decision taken against the market on the day rather than at the next report, and the replacement side of it is not static either.

On training, four fit. After the S114: capitalisation & EFS, which is written for exactly the position Table 15 describes. LOBO loans (legacy) for the £8m. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice, given Table 9 runs to 2028 and the indicator is where CIPFA is heading. And PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator for the pricing above. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
